newsitem.title: FRANCE: France says lira should rise before ERM reentry.
newsitem.headline: France says lira should rise before ERM reentry.

text.p: France said on Wednesday it wanted Italy to be among the founder members of a single European currency but the lira must first "catch up" with the franc.

President Jacques Chirac's spokeswoman, Catherine Colonna, sought to clarify Paris' position after Chirac triggered a diplomatic row with Rome on Tuesday by saying Italy might not be fit to join European monetary union from the start in 1999.

Colonna told reporters Italy's ability to be in the first wave of single currency members hinged partly on its early re-entry into the European Monetary System's exchange rate mechanism (ERM) at a more appropriate exchange rate.

"We want the lira to rejoin the ERM rapidly. Some people have talked about the coming months, perhaps even before the end of the year. That seems to us a good thing. But in any case it must occur at an appropriate level...and there is undoubtedly some catching-up to do," she said.
Chirac's comments had infuriated the Italian government just after it adopted a tough austerity budget in a last-ditch bid to qualify against the odds for the single currency.

The president retreated later on Tuesday, praising Italy's budget and saying he hoped it would be in the first wave of monetary union, after Rome protested and threatened to cancel a Franco-Italian summit due to start in Naples on Thursday night.
The lira's weakness has been a bone of contention between Italy and other European countries ever since the Italian currency crashed out of the ERM in 1992.
Chirac vociferously echoed French businessmen in blaming a cheap lira for hurting French industry and triggering a flood of car and textile imports.

Economists and government officials say the exchange rate at which the lira re-enters the ERM is crucial, since it is likely to determine the competitiveness of Italian exports within a future single currency zone, whenever Italy joins.

Analysts say influential French and German policymakers fear that if Italy is in European monetary union from the outset, the weakness of its public finances could undermine the euro's strength and force up interest rates as Europe seeks to establish the currency's credibility in financial markets.

Publicly, European officials say Italy and other so called peripheral countries, disparagingly dubbed the "Club Med", must not be pre-judged and that if they meet the criteria in the Maastricht treaty, they can join.

But economists believe Germany would prefer a narrower EMU membership to ensure the new euro is as stable as the mark. France's position is less clear, since French ministers have, for example, praised Spain's efforts to make the grade.
Colonna said the lira had depreciated by about 40 percent against the franc after it was ejected from the ERM and had since regained about 18 percent of its value.
"The movement of the lira in the past year is positive but it is no secret that we think there is still room for appreciation (against the franc)," Colonna said.
One influential French industrialist, PSA Peugeot Citroen chairman Jacques Calvet, said on Tuesday the lira was still undervalued and demanded it strengthen.
But rival Italian carmaker Fiat's deputy chairman Roberto Testore retorted that the lira was now overvalued.
Testore told reporters he estimated the right level at 1,040 lira to the German mark. At 1015 GMT on Wednesday, the lira was trading at 996.20 per mark.
Eric Chaney, economist with Morgan Stanley in Paris, said the current lira level was in line with a 20-year average rate and fairly reflected its value in broad macroeconomic terms.
Disputing the argument that a cheap lira had distorted Franco-Italian trade, he said: "The currency factors are only at the margin."
